## Statement

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $a,\mu,\rho_0>0$, $p_\infty\in\mathbb R$, $U\in\mathbb R^3$, and $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$. On the exterior domain $\Omega_a=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:r=|x|>a\}$ put $s=U\cdot x$ and define

$$u(x)=A(r)U+B(r)sx,\qquad A(r)=1-\frac{3a}{4r}-\frac{a^3}{4r^3},\qquad B(r)=-\frac{3a}{4r^3}+\frac{3a^3}{4r^5},\qquad p(x)=p_\infty-\frac{3\mu a}{2}\frac{s}{r^3}.$$

This field is $C^2$ up to the spherical boundary from the exterior, $p$ is $C^1$, $u=0$ at $r=a$, and $u\to U$ uniformly in direction as $r\to\infty$. It satisfies the steady Stokes system $\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0$, $\operatorname{div}u=0$ on $\Omega_a$. For $n=x/a$ on $S_a=\{x:|x|=a\}$, put $D u=(\partial_j u_i)_{i,j}$ and form the stress $\sigma=-pI_3+\mu(Du+(Du)^{\mathsf T})$. The formal resultant with this sphere orientation is

$$\int_{S_a}\sigma n\,dS=6\pi\mu aU.$$

Moreover, among classical pairs $(\widetilde u,\widetilde p)$ satisfying the same Stokes system on $\Omega_a$, the same zero boundary velocity and far-field limits, and the uniform decay conditions $\widetilde u-U=O(r^{-1})$, $\nabla\widetilde u=O(r^{-2})$, $\widetilde p-p_\infty=O(r^{-2})$, this pair is unique. Here the velocity is $C^2$ and pressure $C^1$ locally up to $S_a$, the displayed bounds hold uniformly in direction, and pressure is normalized by its limit $p_\infty$. The claim is for the Stokes equations only; it gives no finite-Reynolds-number error bound or exterior Navier–Stokes existence result. Under SI interpretation, $a,r,x$ are in metres, $U$ in metres per second, $\rho_0$ in kilograms per cubic metre, $\mu$ in pascal-seconds, $\nu$ in square metres per second, $p,p_\infty$ in pascals, and the resultant in newtons.

## Statement references

[Iain W. Stewart, MIT 8.09/8.309, Chapter 6, §6.8](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-09-classical-mechanics-iii-fall-2014/d9bac33f6c60b304dc0398e99b327102_MIT8_09F14_full.pdf)

[David Tong, Fluid Mechanics lecture notes, Chapter 2, §§3.4.1–3.4.2](https://davidtong.org/pdfs/teaching/fluid-mechanics/fluids2.pdf)

Cartesian derivative, Stokes-system, and stress conventions: [[def-fd-x00]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Use the sphere, constants, fields, boundary values, far-field limits, regularity and uniform decay conditions stated above. All equations and the stress resultant are formal mathematical model quantities.

[F1] [[def-fd-x00]]: the constant-density steady Stokes equation is $\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0$ with $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$; $D u=(\partial_j u_i)_{i,j}$, $\Delta$ is componentwise, and the stress is $-pI_3+\mu(Du+(Du)^{\mathsf T})$.

[F2] [[thm-divergence-theorem-for-bounded-c-one-euclidean-domains]]: under $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, the divergence theorem holds for a bounded $C^1$ Euclidean domain and a $C^1$ vector field on its closure, with outward normal on every boundary component.

[A1] [[def-countable-choice]]: assume the indexed axiom of countable choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ used by [F2].

[F3] [[def-first-fundamental-form-and-surface-area-density]]: the surface density is the nonnegative square root of the determinant of the Gram matrix of the parameter tangents.

[F4] [[def-surface-area-and-scalar-surface-integral-of-a-patch]]: a continuous scalar field is integrated against that density on the parameter region; area is the integral of the density, and changing values on a content-zero parameter boundary does not change the integral. Vector integrals are evaluated componentwise.

## Proof

1.1 For any radial scalar functions $A,B$, direct Cartesian differentiation with $\partial_i r=x_i/r$ and $\partial_i s=U_i$ gives $\operatorname{div}(AU+Bsx)=(s/r)(A'+r^2B'+4rB)$ and $\Delta(AU+Bsx)=(A''+2A'/r+2B)U+(B''+6B'/r)sx$. For the stated coefficients, $A'=3a/(4r^2)+3a^3/(4r^4)$, $A''=-3a/(2r^3)-3a^3/r^5$, $B'=9a/(4r^4)-15a^3/(4r^6)$, and $B''=-9a/r^5+45a^3/(2r^7)$. Substitution yields $A'+r^2B'+4rB=0$ and $\Delta u=-3aU/(2r^3)+9asx/(2r^5)$. Also $\nabla(s/r^3)=U/r^3-3sx/r^5$, so $\nabla p=\mu\Delta u$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 At $r=a$, $A(a)=B(a)=0$, giving $u=0$. As $r\to\infty$, $A(r)-1=O(r^{-1})$ and $|B(r)sx|=O(r^{-1})$ uniformly because $|s|\le |U|r$; hence $u-U=O(r^{-1})$. Differentiating the displayed radial expression gives $\nabla u=O(r^{-2})$, and $|p-p_\infty|\le (3\mu a|U|)/(2r^2)$; these also establish the required uniform far-field limits. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

2.2 Let $(\widetilde u,\widetilde p)$ be any other pair in the stated class and put $w=\widetilde u-u$, $q=\widetilde p-p$. Subtracting the equations gives $\operatorname{div}w=0$, $\mu\Delta w=\nabla q$, $w=0$ on $S_a$, and $w=O(r^{-1})$, $\nabla w=O(r^{-2})$, $q=O(r^{-2})$ uniformly. For each $R>a$, apply [F2] on the bounded smooth annulus $\Omega_{a,R}=\{a<r<R\}$ to $qw$ and to $\sum_iw_i\nabla w_i$. The product rule and $\operatorname{div}w=0$ give $\int_{\Omega_{a,R}}w\cdot\nabla q=\int_{\partial\Omega_{a,R}}q\,w\cdot n_R\,dS$ and $\int_{\Omega_{a,R}}w\cdot\Delta w=\int_{\partial\Omega_{a,R}}w\cdot\partial_{n_R}w\,dS-\int_{\Omega_{a,R}}|\nabla w|^2dx$. Substitution into $\mu\Delta w=\nabla q$ yields $\mu\int_{\Omega_{a,R}}|\nabla w|^2dx=\int_{r=R}(\mu w\cdot\partial_rw-q\,w\cdot n)\,dS$, since both inner-boundary terms vanish by $w=0$. [given, F2, A1, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 Write $U_t=U-(U\cdot n)n$ on $S_a$. There $A'(a)=3/(2a)$, $B(a)=0$, and $B'(a)=-3/(2a^3)$, so the outward radial derivative is $\partial_nu=(3/(2a))U_t$. Since the boundary trace is the zero vector, every tangential derivative there vanishes; thus $Du=(3/(2a))U_t\otimes n$, $(Du)^{\mathsf T}n=0$, and $Du\,n=(3/(2a))U_t$. Further, $p|_{S_a}=p_\infty-(3\mu/(2a))(U\cdot n)$. It follows that $\sigma n=-p_\infty n+(3\mu/(2a))U$. [given, F1, step 2.1, algebra]

4.1 For $\Phi(\theta,\varphi)=a(\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\sin\theta\sin\varphi,\cos\theta)$, $0\le\theta\le\pi$, $0\le\varphi\le2\pi$, direct differentiation gives tangent Gram coefficients $E=a^2$, $F=0$, $G=a^2\sin^2\theta$. By [F3], the surface density is $\sqrt{EG-F^2}=a^2\sin\theta$ (also $|\Phi_\theta\times\Phi_\varphi|$). The spherical chart is regular in the parameter interior, with the poles and seam on its content-zero parameter boundary. By [F4] those boundary values contribute zero to the integral, so $\operatorname{area}(S_a)=a^2\int_0^{2\pi}\int_0^\pi\sin\theta\,d\theta\,d\varphi=4\pi a^2$. The parameter change $(\theta,\varphi)\mapsto(\pi-\theta,\varphi+\pi\bmod2\pi)$ has absolute Jacobian one on each half of the longitude interval, preserves the density since $\sin(\pi-\theta)=\sin\theta$, and induces the antipodal map. Thus the antipodal map $n\mapsto-n$ preserves spherical area and reverses $n$, so $\int_{S_a}n\,dS=0$. Integrating the expression in step 3.1 and using $\operatorname{area}(S_a)=4\pi a^2$ gives $\int_{S_a}\sigma n\,dS=(3\mu/(2a))4\pi a^2U=6\pi\mu aU$. [F3, F4, step 3.1, construct, algebra]

5.1 On $r=R$ the integrand in step 2.2 is $O(R^{-3})$ and the area is $4\pi R^2$, so its integral tends to zero as $R\to\infty$. The left side is nonnegative and nondecreasing in $R$; since it equals a quantity tending to zero, it is zero for every $R>a$. Continuity then gives $\nabla w=0$ throughout the connected exterior, so $w$ is constant there; its far-field limit is zero, hence $w=0$. The equation now gives $\nabla q=0$, so $q$ is constant, and its zero far-field limit gives $q=0$. [step 2.2, step 4.1, algebra] ∎

## Statement

Let $\rho_0,\mu>0$, $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$, and $U\in\mathbb R$. Use the constant-density incompressible model

$$\partial_tu+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0,\qquad \operatorname{div}u=0,$$

with Cartesian derivatives and componentwise Laplacian; its unsteady Stokes system omits the convective term. Set $I=(0,\infty)$ and $\Omega_+=\mathbb R\times(0,\infty)\times\mathbb R$, with coordinates $(x,y,z)$. Define $I_0=\int_0^\infty e^{-r^2}\,dr$ and $E(s)=I_0^{-1}\int_s^\infty e^{-r^2}\,dr$ for $s\ge0$. On $I\times\Omega_+$ define $u:I\times\Omega_+\to\mathbb R^3$ by $u(t,x,y,z)=(U E(y/(2\sqrt{\nu t})),0,0)$ and let $p$ be any constant scalar field. The field is smooth for $t>0,y>0$ and satisfies the pointwise unsteady Stokes equation $\partial_tu+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0$ and $\operatorname{div}u=0$. It also solves the full constant-density Navier–Stokes system because its convective term vanishes. For each fixed $t>0$ and $x,z\in\mathbb R$, its one-sided boundary limit is $\lim_{y\downarrow0}u(t,x,y,z)=(U,0,0)$ and its limit as $y\to\infty$ is $0$; for each fixed $x,z\in\mathbb R$ and $y>0$, its limit as $t\downarrow0$ is $0$. The corner $(t,y)=(0,0)$ is excluded from the classical claim. For every $x,z\in\mathbb R$, $t>0$, $0<\varepsilon<1$, and $y\ge2\sqrt{\nu t}\sqrt{\log(1/\varepsilon)}$, the absolute value of the first velocity component satisfies $|U E(y/(2\sqrt{\nu t}))|\le\varepsilon|U|$.

Separately, let $\mathbb T_L=\mathbb R/(L\mathbb Z)$ for $L>0$, set $\mathbb T^3=\mathbb T_{L_x}\times\mathbb T_{L_y}\times\mathbb T_{L_z}$, and let $\pi:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb T^3$ be the quotient map, where $L_x,L_y,L_z>0$. Equip this quotient with the flat smooth structure and metric induced by Euclidean translations, identifying each tangent space with $\mathbb R^3$ through the derivative of $\pi$. In this branch, the Navier–Stokes equations mean that the periodic lift satisfies the displayed constant-density system pointwise on $\mathbb R^3$. Choose an integer $m\ge1$, put $k=2\pi m/L_y$, and let $A\in\mathbb R$. The periodic lift $\widetilde u(t,x,y,z)=(A e^{-\nu k^2t}\sin(ky),0,0)$ defines a smooth vector field $u$ on $\mathbb T^3$ by $u(t,\pi(q))=d\pi_q(\widetilde u(t,q))$; with constant pressure, it is an exact Navier–Stokes solution for all $t\in\mathbb R$. Choose $c,b>0$ with $c<L_x/2$, $b<L_y/2$, and $0<\alpha:=kb<\pi$. Define the closed lifted loop and its quotient by

$$\widetilde X(t,s)=\left(c\sin(2\pi s)+\frac{A}{\nu k^2}(1-e^{-\nu k^2t})\sin(kb\cos(2\pi s)),\,b\cos(2\pi s),\,0\right),\qquad X(t,s)=\pi(\widetilde X(t,s)),\quad t\in\mathbb R,\quad 0\le s\le1.$$

The displayed lift satisfies $\widetilde X(t,0)=\widetilde X(t,1)$. The loop is material when $\partial_t\widetilde X(t,s)=\widetilde u(t,\widetilde X(t,s))$, as it does here. Define its flat-torus circulation by $\Gamma(t)=\int_0^1\widetilde u(t,\widetilde X(t,s))\cdot\partial_s\widetilde X(t,s)\,ds$; this value is unchanged if the lift is translated by a vector in $L_x\mathbb Z\times L_y\mathbb Z\times L_z\mathbb Z$. Let $C_\alpha=\int_0^{2\pi}\cos\theta\,\sin(\alpha\cos\theta)\,d\theta$. Then $C_\alpha>0$ and $\Gamma(t)=AcC_\alpha e^{-\nu k^2t}$, which is nonconstant when $A\ne0$. The corner-excluded wall-layer solution and periodic material-loop solution are distinct exact mathematical models; neither states an experiment or a general boundary-layer theorem. Under SI interpretation, $x,y,z,L_x,L_y,L_z,b,c$ are in metres, $t$ in seconds, $u,U,A$ in metres per second, $\rho_0$ in kilograms per cubic metre, $\mu$ in pascal-seconds, $\nu$ in square metres per second, and $k$ in inverse metres.

## Statement references

[Shreyas Mandre, Fluid Dynamics Lecture Notes, Chapter 3, §3.3.1](https://notes.shreyasmandre.com/fluid-dynamics-notes/Ch3.html)

[MIT 2.25 Advanced Fluid Mechanics, Solution to Stokes First Problem ATP](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/2-25-advanced-fluid-mechanics-fall-2013/6c64b72340cd5b5da9a0d59516b63aec_MIT2_25F13_SolutionStokes1.pdf)

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Use the constants, domains, velocities, initial and wall limits, loop orientation and regularity in the Statement. The equations are pointwise formal model equations; the first solution is classical only for $t>0,y>0$.

[F1] [[def-fd-x00]]: for constant density, $\nu=\mu/\rho_0$ and the incompressible Navier–Stokes equation is $u_t+(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p-\nu\Delta u=0$ with $\operatorname{div}u=0$; Cartesian derivatives and componentwise Laplacian are used. This supplies the pointwise system for the half-space field and, through the periodic-lift convention in the Statement, for the torus field. The Euclidean material-loop definition there has domain in an open subset of $\mathbb R^3$; it is not used for the torus loop, whose material condition and circulation are defined through lifts in the Statement.

[A1] On the first domain the pressure is constant. On the torus, $A$ and $k$ are constant and the displayed field is periodic because $kL_y=2\pi m$.

## Proof

1.1 The Gaussian integral $I_0$ is positive and finite: its integrand is positive and, for $r\ge1$, $e^{-r^2}\le e^{-r}$, whose tail is integrable. Differentiation gives $E'(s)=-e^{-s^2}/I_0$ and $E''(s)=-2sE'(s)$. For $s=y/(2\sqrt{\nu t})$, $s_t=-s/(2t)$ and $s_y=1/(2\sqrt{\nu t})$, so $u_t=-UsE'(s)/(2t)$ and $\nu u_{yy}=-UsE'(s)/(2t)$. Thus $u_t=\nu u_{yy}$; the field has zero divergence and zero convection because it has only an $x$ component and is independent of $x$. The pressure gradient is zero, so [F1] gives the exact equation. Also $E(0)=1$, $E(s)\to0$ as $s\to\infty$, and for fixed $y>0$, $s\to\infty$ as $t\downarrow0$. [given, F1, A1, algebra]

1.2 For the periodic lift, $\partial_t\widetilde u=-\nu k^2\widetilde u$, $\Delta\widetilde u=-k^2\widetilde u$, $\operatorname{div}\widetilde u=0$, and $(\widetilde u\cdot\nabla)\widetilde u=\widetilde u_x\partial_x\widetilde u=0$. A constant pressure therefore makes every term in [F1] sum to zero. Let $y_0(s)=b\cos(2\pi s)$ and $x_0(s)=c\sin(2\pi s)$; the displacement $d(y,t)=A(1-e^{-\nu k^2t})\sin(ky)/(\nu k^2)$ satisfies $d_t(y,t)=Ae^{-\nu k^2t}\sin(ky)$. Hence $\widetilde X(t,s)=(x_0(s)+d(y_0(s),t),y_0(s),0)$ is closed and $\partial_t\widetilde X=\widetilde u(t,\widetilde X)$, so its quotient $X=\pi\circ\widetilde X$ is a smooth material loop. Translating the lift by a lattice vector changes neither its derivative nor the periodic velocity, proving the stated lift invariance. Its circulation is $\int_0^1Ae^{-\nu k^2t}\sin(ky_0(s))(x_0'(s)+d_y(y_0(s),t)y_0'(s))\,ds$. ## Statement

Let $a,\rho_0>0$, $p_\infty\in\mathbb R$, $U\in\mathbb R^3$, and on $\Omega_a=\{x\in\mathbb R^3:r=|x|>a\}$ define $n=x/r$, $\phi(x)=(U\cdot x)(1+a^3/(2r^3))$, $u=\nabla\phi$, and $p=p_\infty+\rho_0(|U|^2-|u|^2)/2$. Then $u,p$ are smooth in the exterior and up to $r=a$, $u\to U$ and $p\to p_\infty$ uniformly in direction at infinity, and $u\cdot n=0$ on $r=a$. The pair solves $(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p=0$, $\operatorname{div}u=0$, the steady formal constant-density incompressible Euler system. Its boundary condition is impermeable slip/no-through: $u$ is generally nonzero tangent to the sphere, so this is not a no-slip solution. For the formal Euler stress $\sigma_E=-pI_3$ and sphere normal $n=x/a$ pointing from the center into the exterior, the exact resultant is

$$\int_{|x|=a}\sigma_E n\,dS=-\int_{|x|=a}p n\,dS=0.$$

The theorem concerns only this explicit inviscid mathematical model; it asserts neither a viscous zero-drag result nor an observed force. Under SI interpretation, $a,r,x$ are in metres, $U,u$ in metres per second, $\rho_0$ in kilograms per cubic metre, and $p,p_\infty$ in pascals.

## Statement references

[Iain W. Stewart, MIT 8.09/8.309, Chapter 6, §6.4](https://ocw.mit.edu/courses/8-09-classical-mechanics-iii-fall-2014/d9bac33f6c60b304dc0398e99b327102_MIT8_09F14_full.pdf)

[David Tong, Fluid Mechanics lecture notes, Chapter 1, §§2.3.2–2.3.3](https://davidtong.org/pdfs/teaching/fluid-mechanics/fluids1.pdf)

Formal constant-density incompressible Euler system and pressure-stress definition: [[def-fd-incompressible-euler-system]].

## Facts & Assumptions

**Given:** Use the constants, exterior domain, potential, velocity and pressure in the Statement. All equations are formal pointwise model equations; the surface resultant uses the stated orientation.

[F1] [[def-fd-x00]]: $\nabla$ and $\Delta$ are Cartesian operators, and smooth scalar fields have commuting mixed partials.

[F2] [[def-fd-incompressible-euler-system]]: the steady inviscid equations are $(u\cdot\nabla)u+\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p=0$, $\operatorname{div}u=0$, and the formal stress is $\sigma_E=-pI_3$ with resultant $\int_S\sigma_En_S\,dS$.

[F3] [[thm-fd-x09]]: for every $C^2$ vector field, $(u\cdot\nabla)u=\nabla(|u|^2/2)-u\times\operatorname{curl}u$. This is the exact algebraic clause of that theorem used here; no barotropic Bernoulli conclusion is invoked.

[F4] [[def-first-fundamental-form-and-surface-area-density]]: the surface density is the nonnegative square root of the determinant of the Gram matrix of the parameter tangents.

[F5] [[def-surface-area-and-scalar-surface-integral-of-a-patch]]: a continuous scalar field is integrated against that density on the parameter region; area is the integral of the density, and changing values on a content-zero parameter boundary does not change the integral. Vector integrals are evaluated componentwise.

## Proof

1.1 For $r>0$, $\partial_i(1/r)=-x_i/r^3$ and $\partial_i^2(1/r)=-1/r^3+3x_i^2/r^5$ for $i=1,2,3$, so $\Delta(1/r)=-3/r^3+3r^2/r^5=0$. Since $(U\cdot x)/r^3=-U\cdot\nabla(1/r)$, commuting smooth derivatives gives $\Delta((U\cdot x)/r^3)=0$. Also $\Delta(U\cdot x)=0$, so $\Delta\phi=0$. Therefore $\operatorname{div}u=\Delta\phi=0$ and $\operatorname{curl}u=0$ by equality of the mixed second partials of $\phi$. Direct differentiation yields $u=U+\frac{a^3}{2r^3}\bigl(U-3(U\cdot n)n\bigr)$. This gives uniform $u\to U$ at infinity. At $r=a$, $u=(3/2)(U-(U\cdot n)n)$, which is tangent to the sphere and has zero normal component. [given, F1, algebra]

2.1 By [F3] and $\operatorname{curl}u=0$, $(u\cdot\nabla)u=\nabla(|u|^2/2)$. The pressure definition gives $\rho_0^{-1}\nabla p=-\nabla(|u|^2/2)$, so the steady momentum equation in [F2] holds; step 1.1 supplies its divergence condition. The explicit formula gives $u-U=O(r^{-1})$, hence $|u|^2\to|U|^2$ and $p\to p_\infty$ uniformly in direction. [given, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 On the sphere, $u=(3/2)U_t$ with $U_t=U-(U\cdot n)n$, so $|u|^2=(9/4)(|U|^2-(U\cdot n)^2)$. Thus $p|_{r=a}$ depends on $n$ only through $(U\cdot n)^2$ and is unchanged by $n\mapsto-n$. For $\Phi(\theta,\varphi)=a(\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\sin\theta\sin\varphi,\cos\theta)$, $0\le\theta\le\pi$, $0\le\varphi\le2\pi$, direct differentiation gives tangent Gram coefficients $E=a^2$, $F=0$, $G=a^2\sin^2\theta$, so [F4] gives density $\sqrt{EG-F^2}=a^2\sin\theta$ (also $|\Phi_\theta\times\Phi_\varphi|$). The chart is regular in the parameter interior, and its poles and seam lie on the content-zero parameter boundary allowed in [F5]; those boundary values do not affect the integral. The substitution $(\theta,\varphi)\mapsto(\pi-\theta,\varphi+\pi\bmod2\pi)$ has absolute Jacobian one on each half of the longitude interval, preserves the density because $\sin(\pi-\theta)=\sin\theta$, and induces the antipodal map, which reverses $n$, so the vector integrand $p n$ has zero integral over the sphere. By the stress convention in [F2], $\int_{|x|=a}\sigma_En\,dS=-\int_{|x|=a}pn\,dS=0$. [given, F2, F4, F5, step 1.1, construct, algebra] ∎

## Remarks

The diagram is a two-dimensional cross-section of the sphere. The radial arrow is the outward unit normal $n$; the tangent arrow indicates the direction of the boundary velocity $u=(3/2)U_t$. The drawing is schematic and is not used in the field-equation or resultant proof.

```tikz
\end{tikzpicture}
```
